scores.evidence: The server confirms an edit only after the commit... An old client that doesn't know a new node type would otherwise delete it
scores.rationale: Yjs/CRDT semantics, commit-before-confirm durability, relative-position anchors, revocation limits of CRDT caching, and compaction-equals-replay checks are all stated accurately, including subtle areas like old-client node deletion.

scores.evidence: A browser-based rich-text editor where several users edit the same document at once and see each other's changes live
scores.rationale: Delivers precisely the requested real-time co-editor with sensible ambiguity resolution (SaaS, online-first) and an explicit, justified deferred list for offline-days, E2EE, search and mobile.

scores.evidence: Content favours availability... Permissions and metadata favour consistency: Postgres is the source of truth
scores.rationale: Clear data ownership (CRDT content vs Postgres metadata), two deployables with a stated reason, and the availability/consistency split is honored consistently in revocation, caching and feature design with no contradictions.

scores.evidence: 0 divergent final states over 10,000 sessions... Under load, kill -9 sync nodes, fail over Postgres and partition Redis
scores.rationale: V1/V2 test the riskiest assumptions before any real content is stored, thresholds are labeled requirement or assumption, and validation continues in production via state-hash divergence alerts and V5 beta telemetry.

scores.evidence: The plan assumes the following. Each one changes the phase order if it is false
scores.rationale: Every number is tagged ASSUMPTION or UNKNOWN with a stated basis, missing inputs name their owner and deadline, and sensitivity (E2EE, offline duration, residency) is spelled out with what changes if wrong.

scores.evidence: A confirmed edit is silently lost, or copies of a document stay different, and users find out only later
scores.rationale: Covers divergence, lost confirmed edits, crash/failover/partition, duplicates and reordering, revocation, cross-tenant leaks, forged tokens, noisy tenants, Redis loss, region loss and compaction corruption, each with concrete detection and recovery.

scores.evidence: Graceful drain on deploy. Clients reconnect with jittered backoff and resend pending edits
scores.rationale: Deploy/rollback pipeline from Phase 0, SLO burn-rate alerts, DR drills, runbooks, an explicit complexity budget (≤4 runtime components, one on-call rotation) and an operations review size the burden to a realistic team.

scores.evidence: Cost per active editor per month: UNKNOWN. Product/finance supplies it from the price point. Needed before Phase 5
scores.rationale: Storage growth budget, cost-per-editor gate before GA, and the build-vs-buy trade-off are covered honestly, but there is no order-of-magnitude estimate of run or engineering cost and scaling-cost reasoning is thin.

scores.evidence: Point of no return: the first real content stored in format v1. V1 and V2 guard it, and both must pass first
scores.rationale: Every decision carries an R2/R3 reversibility tag with a revisit trigger and exit path (Automerge/OT flip, managed vendor, per-tenant DB), and the irreversible format commitment is validated before it is made.

scores.evidence: ≤ 4 runtime components (web/API, sync, Postgres, Redis) plus object storage, with one on-call rotation
scores.rationale: The design is the simplest that meets the need, enforces its own complexity budget, defers speculative scope (multi-region, search, enterprise SSO) with pull-forward triggers, and omits nothing essential.

scores.evidence: V1 finds a divergence that can't be fixed in the binding → Automerge or a server-sequenced OT design (re-plan Phase 1)
scores.rationale: Phases are ordered by dependency and rework width with checkable exit criteria, Phase 0 gives a concrete first slice, and every validation states what happens if it fails.
